visible.summary:
Germany's Pride movement faces a documented rise in attacks: the amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-motivated attacks on Pride events nationally in 2024 and 30 in 2025 across roughly 120 parades, including a boiling-water attack, and runs a €100,000 support fund weighted to eastern Germany. Ahead of the 2025 Christopher Street Day, with hundreds of thousands expected, Berlin's organisers nonetheless urged participants to 'be vigilant'.

The reporting also situates the capital: Maneo, Berlin's anti-violence documentation project, states that big-city parades like Berlin's had not been specifically threatened — smaller towns are hardest to police — while everyday hostility still surfaces: one Berlin-Neukölln queer café owner reports 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in eighteen months.
visible.tangentialFactors: The Guardian's Berlin-side evidence (Maneo's documentation of homophobic violence, the Neukölln café's 45 complaints about anti-gay attacks) concerns LGB-targeted hostility in the city rather than trans-specific incidents — an indicator of general queer visibility risk, not of trans-directed enforcement.

sources.claim: The Guardian (26 July 2025) on German Pride parades facing a rise in attacks: Berlin CSD organisers urge vigilance with hundreds of thousands expected; the amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-extremist attacks on Pride events nationally in 2024 and 30 so far in 2025 across ~120 parades (including an attack with boiling water), and runs a €100,000 CSD support fund focused on eastern Germany; Maneo, the Berlin anti-violence documentation project, states big-city parades like Berlin and Cologne were not specifically threatened and that smaller towns are hardest to police; a Berlin-Neukölln queer café owner reports 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in 18 months.

MANEO, Berlin's anti-violence documentation project, states that it recorded 723 LSBTIQ+-hostile incidents in Berlin in 2025, slightly fewer than the 738 documented in 2024, from 1,014 new reports - a new high; its 12 May 2026 release lists insults, threats and physical attacks in public transport, parks and streets, with Schöneberg, Neukölln, Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain and Tiergarten most affected, plus 58 attacks on LSBTIQ+ venues, memorials and events. MANEO says the figures capture only part of reality because of a high dark figure, and that the counselling centre itself was attacked several times in 2025. This is the primary Berlin project behind the record's claim that documented homophobic violence in the capital is rising, and it names Neukölln - the record's café-owner example - among the worst-hit districts.

MANEO reports that at the 48th Berlin Christopher Street Day a vehicle drove into a crowd in the Tiergarten area, killing one woman, injuring several people and forcing the event to be cancelled; the project offers victim counselling and an anonymous reporting line (030-2163336, daily 17:00-19:00). This is a dated, outcome-specific Berlin Pride incident - evidence that the serious attack risk the record's 2025 'be vigilant' organisers warned about has materialised at the capital's own CSD.

The Berlin state government's official prison-service page states that legislation has created a basis for considering trans, inter* and non-binary people held in custody, that Berlin prison staff are responsible for taking each detainee's individual needs into account within the legal framework, and it details gender-segregated placement, intake procedures and counselling and support offers. This is Berlin-specific official information on how the capital's prison administration (JVA Moabit, JVA für Frauen Berlin, etc.) treats trans/inter/non-binary detainees, the detention-side counterpart to the city's anti-queer violence statistics.

visible.summary:
In Cottbus on 20 October 2025, a rubbish container was set alight against the façade of the 'Regenbogenkombinat' queer cultural centre during CSD week; the fire was out in about fifteen minutes and nobody was hurt, but state security (Staatsschutz) took over the arson investigation and a political motive cannot be excluded — local initiatives call it an attempted firebombing, and the attack sits among earlier suspected far-right attacks in the city.

The subsequent Cottbus CSD — the 17th edition, under the motto 'Vereint in Frieden und Vielfalt' — ran with a large police presence against two registered far-right counter-demonstrations, one organised by 'Deutsche Jugend voran', and proceeded without major disruption. The local queer community describes itself as unusually watchful: repeated physical pressure on infrastructure, met by a functioning protective response.
visible.tangentialFactors: The counter-mobilisations and the 2026 "sign against the right" framing centre on far-right hostility to Pride/queer visibility generally (CSD counter-demos, union coalitions) rather than on trans-specific action — but they define the street climate a visibly queer visitor enters in the Cottbus area.

sources.claim: Lausitzer Rundschau: ahead of the CSD in Cottbus a fire (Regenbogenkombinat) prompted a state-security (Staatsschutz) investigation; the paper covers Cottbus and the surrounding Lausitz region.
Niederlausitz aktuell (26 October 2025): the CSD parade in Cottbus proceeded with a large police deployment and two counter-demos.

visible.summary:
A Hessen Landtag small inquiry with the Interior Minister's answer (April 2025) records police-registered queer-hostile offences rising from 33 in 2022 to 83 in 2023 and 135 in 2024 — a year-on-year jump of 52 that the minister's reply calls alarming.

The trend must be read with the federal BKA's own caveat: its situation report on LSBTIQ* security introduced a new reporting category that makes state-by-state comparison possible but warns that classification changes can inflate registered counts, so rises may partly reflect better recording rather than a sharper danger. The same answer notes the 2010-established network of LSBTIQ* liaison officers in every police headquarters, governed by a standing framework concept — an institutional response in place while the statistics remain ambiguous.
visible.tangentialFactors: The recorded rise covers queer-hostile crime generally — the KPMD category combines hostility to sexual orientation and to gender-related diversity — so the trend is a general negative-climate signal rather than a trans-specific series.

sources.claim: Hessen Landtag small inquiry and Interior Minister answer (April 2025): police-registered queer-hostile offences in Hessen rose from 33 (2022) to 83 (2023) and to 135 (2024, +52 year-on-year — described as alarming); notes LSBTIQ* liaison officers established in all police headquarters since 2010 and a framework concept governing them.

Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) situation report on the security of LSBTIQ* people in Germany, published with the Interior Ministry: a multi-year rise in police-registered queer-hostile offences and the new federal reporting category that makes Land-by-Land comparison possible; classification changes can inflate Land counts, so cross-Land numbers need caution.

hessenschau reports (21 August 2025) that the Hessian interior ministry's answer to a Landtag inquiry by three Grüne MPs recorded 135 queer-hostile offences in Hessen in 2024, 52 more than the previous year, among them 16 cases of dangerous grievous bodily harm, seven of bodily harm, 13 of property damage and 26 of insult, with many victims not reporting so that a high dark figure is assumed. Interior Minister Roman Poseck (CDU) called the development 'alarmierend', attributed part of the responsibility to far-right forces, and the ministry counted suspects identified in 46 of the 2024 proceedings and six convictions. This is the media confirmation of the record's police-registered 33 (2022) to 83 (2023) to 135 (2024) series.

hessenschau reports (17 May 2026) from a further Poseck answer to a Grüne Landtag inquiry that Hessen police counted 141 queer-hostile offences in 2025, against 83 in 2023 and 33 in 2022 - a more than fourfold rise within four years that Poseck called 'alarmierend' and only 'the tip of the iceberg' given the high dark figure; he cited a January 2026 Kassel tram incident in which a male couple was homophobically insulted, threatened and spat on. The article notes Hessen police keep dedicated contact officers for this hate crime and the state government promises consistent prosecution. It updates the record's statistics with the 2025 figure of 141 and confirms the state's own alarm at the trend.

Resident Advisor reports (20 June 2025) that trans woman artist BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act after a male security officer refused her a search by a female officer during screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024 and told her she was 'not a woman'; Frankfurt Airport later apologised by email, said the security service provider had been instructed to investigate, and promised security staff would be trained on dealing with transgender and gender non-conforming travellers. This is a dated, jurisdiction-specific case of transphobic treatment at Hessen's main international airport - the first screening-gate incident evidence for this record.

visible.summary:
Northern Ireland carries three sub-national negatives absent elsewhere in the UK: Education Minister Paul Givan ordered the 2019 transgender-pupils guidance withdrawn from the Education Authority website in September 2025 after the FWS ruling, calling it "unlawful and flawed" and a product of "activist campaigns"; the Justice Minister's attempt to include transgender people as a protected group in hate-crime sentencing reform was stalled (reported DUP obstruction); and the Rainbow Project records a pattern of paramilitary-flavoured anti-LGB&T violence including a pipe bomb thrown through the home of a trans woman in Derry/Londonderry described by PSNI as a "sectarian hate crime," a 2019 Belfast city-centre assault hospitalising a gay man, and an average of ~290 anti-LGB&T incidents per year (2013–2017) with rising transgender-identity strand counts to September 2025.

Counter-balancing: PSNI/NISRA track a separate "transgender identity" category (unlike England and Wales), evidencing institutional recognition; the Health Minister publicly defended gender-identity service funding (£800k+ uplift) against DUP/TUV criticism, showing the executive is split rather than uniformly hostile. No criminal ban on expression or police-enforced facility prohibition exists — the risk mechanism mirrors the national EHRC code (service refusal by staff) plus street-level violence.
visible.tangentialFactors: The violence record mixes anti-gay and anti-trans incidents (the 2019 Belfast assault was anti-gay; the ~290/year series counts anti-LGB&T broadly) — the trans strand is smaller but separately tracked and rising.
visible.localsOnly: The withdrawn school guidance bore on trans pupils in resident families; the stalled protected-group reform concerns sentencing for offences against residents — a visitor encounters both as climate and policing-culture signals rather than direct machinery.

sources.claim: BBC News (8 September 2025): guidance supporting transgender pupils was withdrawn from the Northern Ireland Education Authority's website after Education Minister Paul Givan requested removal, arguing it conflicted with departmental policy and the law in Northern Ireland; the guidance had recommended that trans pupils be allowed to use changing rooms matching their gender identity, and teachers' representatives warned removal 'ignores the practical realities'.

BBC News (14 December 2025): other executive parties blocked justice minister Naomi Long's plan to add transgender people as a protected characteristic in Northern Ireland's new hate-crime legislation (approval sought early November, response deadline mid-November; bill had executive agreement from December 2024). Long cited PSNI statistics of close to 100 transgender-identity incidents or hate crimes.

visible.summary:
The Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025 (No. 27 of 2025, assented 30 October 2025; Part 3 in force 27 July 2026) removed the civil provision making it unlawful to "offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate" a person in public on the basis of a protected attribute, including gender identity. The NT is the only Australian jurisdiction that has actively reversed anti-discrimination protection rather than extended it; the government framed the rollback as "restoring freedom of speech and religion." For a visitor, public verbal abuse or humiliation directed at gender expression is now deliberately outside NT law while other states have brought it inside.

Federal protections continue to apply uniformly: the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 covers gender identity in every state and territory, and NT hate-crime penalty enhancements for SO/GI-motivated offences (2022 amendment, effective 2023) remain in force. No criminal expression ban, no facility-access ban, and no conversion-practice-specific enforcement issue arises for a short-term visitor beyond the general federal framework.

Remote-area context amplifies practical risk: Alice Springs records approximately 2,600+ offences against a population of ~25,000, and trans community infrastructure in the NT is thin. A single domestic killing of a Tiwi Sistergirl (Darwin, October 2024) is recorded for completeness but is one non-patterned incident and does not support a regional violence finding on its own.

Vs the national score of 0.86, the NT sits 0.09 below: the deliberate legislative removal of the "offend, insult, humiliate" protection is the strongest negative sub-national signal in Australia, even though it is a civil-law rollback rather than a criminal prohibition. Vs Victoria (0.88), where the 2025 Anti-Vilification Act created the country's first criminal offence for public incitement against a trans person, the NT moved in the opposite direction in the same year.
visible.tangentialFactors: The removed civil provision protects every attribute (race, religion, sexuality, gender identity) — its repeal signals a broad de-protection climate; gender identity is one named attribute rather than the sole target.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The NT's high general assault statistics affect all travellers equally; they appear here only as thin-support and infrastructure context, not as a trans-specific mechanism.

sources.claim: NT legislation page for the assented Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025 (No. 27 of 2025, assented 30 October 2025; Part 3 commencing 27 July 2026), which removes the civil prohibition on offending, insulting, humiliating or intimidating a person in public because of a protected attribute, including gender identity.

ABC News, 17 Oct 2025: the NT government's anti-discrimination amendments passed parliament, framed as restoring free speech and religious freedom — narrowing the vilification provision and letting religious schools prefer staff sharing the same faith; the government had earlier backtracked from scrapping the vilification section. Marks reduced territorial vilification/discipline protections shaping discrimination exposure for visitors.

The jurisdiction status page documents the NT timeline behind this record's assessment: male homosexual activity legal since 1 January 1984 with an equal age of consent since 2003; same-sex marriage from nationwide December 2017 (the territory's postal-survey 'Yes' was 60.6%); full adoption rights since 2018; birth-certificate sex-marker change requiring clinical treatment since 2018; and territory discrimination protections since 2022, with a March 2025 government announcement and July 2025 bill to repeal the vilification ('offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate') provision. It also records that the NT government banned rainbow pride flags in public hospitals in February 2025, issued a policy directive in December 2025 banning gender-affirming healthcare for minors, and that the territory's own hate-crime statute does not list sexual orientation or gender identity (federal coverage of those motives only since 2025). The page independently corroborates the record's central claim that the NT is actively reversing, not extending, anti-discrimination protection.

ABC News, 2 March 2025: the Country Liberal Party government confirmed it would repeal the vilification provision Labor added to NT anti-discrimination law three years earlier, which made it unlawful to 'offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate' a person because of a characteristic such as race or gender and could trigger action by the NT Anti-Discrimination Commission; Attorney-General Marie-Clare Boothby framed the change as restoring 'freedom of speech and religion', including letting religious schools again hire only co-religionists. NT Anti-Discrimination Commissioner Jeswynn Yogaratnam publicly rebuked the move, warning the government may be 'opening the doors for a very dangerous stream of hate speech'. This is the March 2025 announcement that set in motion the rollback this record describes, which the Wikipedia/legislation trail confirms was enacted as the Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025 (assented 30 October 2025).

visible.summary:
Castilla y León is the only Spanish autonomous community that has never enacted a regional LGTBI or gender-identity law, and for a transgender visitor that vacuum has a practical administrative meaning: no dedicated regional equality office exists to receive a complaint, there is no institutional hate-crime observatory, and no region-specific administrative protocol governs responses to gender-motivated incidents. No criminal ban or facility restriction exists in the region, national criminal law fully applies, and the severity floor is therefore set by the state; the recorded deviation of approximately −0.07 from the national score (0.88) reflects sub-national administrative coldness and rural exposure rather than any region-specific criminal threat.

The pending regional LGTBI+ equality bill (registered December 2024, in processing since 11 June 2025) is framed around ending the sexilio — the documented exodus of LGBT people, especially the young, from the region's rural areas to larger cities — a resident-facing concern rather than a visitor protection; until it is enacted, a transgender traveller facing discrimination has no dedicated regional channel beyond the national institutions, and the protective infrastructure is thinnest in the rural areas where the exodus pattern is documented.
visible.tangentialFactors:
Legislative flux: the bill proposed by the opposition PSOE group reached processing on 11 June 2025 only after the governing PP abstained and Vox voted alone against; Vox is on record rejecting LGTBI subsidies in the region, and LGBTI advocates fear the process could stall in committee.

Neighbour comparisons: Madrid (0.84), which at least operated a trans law and a law against anti-LGBT hostility before narrowing them, shows a rollback pattern this region never had a framework to narrow; the other two non-legislating communities, Ceuta and Melilla (0.85), present a statute-book-only gap with no incident evidence, whereas the larger deviation of Castilla y León rests on its documented rural-exodus pattern compounding the absence of protective infrastructure.
visible.localsOnly: The sexilio pattern is resident-facing in its essentials: a documented exodus of LGBT people, especially the young, from the region's rural areas to larger cities, sustained by the same vacuum a visitor would notice — no regional equality office, hate-crime observatory or administrative protocol for residents' complaints. The pending LGTBI+ equality bill answers regional LGBTI+ collectives' long-standing demands, while a visitor's exposure stays governed by state law.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Whether the pending bill advances or stalls in committee was unresolved at reporting time. No visitor documents, border-screening practice, or marriage/partner-travel finding specific to this region is recorded in the dossier.

sources.claim: Europa Press (Valladolid, 11 Jun 2025): the Cortes de Castilla y León voted to take the PSOE-sponsored LGTBI+ bill into consideration (76 articles) after the PP abstained; the bill answers regional LGBTI+ collectives' long-standing demands.

Salamancahoy (20 Dec 2024): the PSOE parliamentary group registered a bill for real and effective equality of LGTBI+ people in Castilla y León, aiming to end the "sexilio" (out-migration of LGBTI people from the region), one of three bills tabled that week; group leader Tudanca urged fastest possible processing.

Diario de Castilla y Leon (11 Jun 2025): the plenary approved taking the LGTBI equality bill into debate with opposition support except Vox and PP abstention; LGBTI advocates fear the process could stall in committee. Same vote as the Europa Press report, adding civil-society reaction.
